scenes.animation: Zippy stands under a grey sky holding a cricket bat, shouting 'If it rain, match cancel!' A giant 'IF' sign drops from the sky and bonks him gently on the head.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: If it rain, match cancel! Why does that sound wrong?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because if-sentences follow patterns. They are called conditionals. Let's learn the three main ones.

scenes.animation: A sentence splits into two coloured blocks: a blue 'if-clause (condition)' and an orange 'main clause (result)'. They swap places, and a comma appears only when the if-clause comes first.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A conditional has two parts. The if-clause gives the condition. The main clause gives the result.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: When the if-clause comes first, put a comma after it. If it rains, we will stay home. We will stay home if it rains.

scenes.animation: Card 1 labelled 'First conditional: real, likely future'. The formula builds: 'If + simple present, will + verb'. Example: 'If it rains, the match will be cancelled.' Dark clouds gather on screen.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The first conditional is for real, likely situations in the future. If plus simple present, then will plus verb.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: If it rains, the match will be cancelled.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So no will in the if-part. Got it!

scenes.animation: Card 2 labelled 'Second conditional: imaginary present'. Formula: 'If + simple past, would + verb'. Zippy imagines himself with a crown. Card 3 labelled 'Third conditional: imaginary past'. Formula: 'If + had + past participle, would have + past participle'. A missed bus drives away.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The second conditional is for imaginary situations now. If plus simple past, then would plus verb. If I were a king, I would build a giant library.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The third conditional is for the past that cannot change. If plus had and past participle, then would have and past participle.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: If I had left earlier, I would have caught the bus.

scenes.animation: A connection card links to The Wit that Won Hearts: Tenali asks 'If the sower yawns, what will happen to the seeds?' The first conditional pattern is highlighted in colour.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Remember Tenali Rama's trick in Unit 1? His whole argument was a conditional. If the sower yawns, the seeds will scatter.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Conditionals help us argue, imagine and regret, all in one tidy pattern.

scenes.animation: A practice card: 'If I ___ (know) the answer, I would tell you.' Options flip: 'know', 'knew', 'had known'. 'knew' glows green. An 'Exam Tip' sticker shows: 'Match the verb in the main clause first'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Try this. If I blank, know, the answer, I would tell you.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Would in the main part means second conditional. So, knew!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Correct. Exam tip: look at the main clause first. Will, would or would have tells you which conditional it is.

scenes.animation: Recap board with three stacked cards: '1. First: If + present, will', '2. Second: If + past, would', '3. Third: If + had + V3, would have + V3'. Zippy, under a clear sky, bats happily.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: first conditional, if plus present, then will, for likely futures.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: second conditional, if plus past, then would, for imaginary situations.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: third conditional, if plus had, then would have, for past regrets.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: If I had learned this earlier, I would have sounded smarter!

scenes.animation: A school canteen. Zippy marches to the counter and demands 'I must get two samosas!' The canteen uncle raises an eyebrow. A thought bubble offers softer options: 'Could I...?', 'May I...?'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I must get two samosas! Why is the canteen uncle frowning?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because must sounds like an order. Words like must, could and may are modals, and each one changes the meaning.

scenes.animation: A toolbox opens. Each tool is a modal with a label: 'can / could: ability', 'may / might: possibility, permission', 'must: necessity', 'should / ought to: advice', 'will / shall: future, promise', 'would: polite request'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Modals are helping verbs that show mood or attitude.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Can and could show ability. May and might show possibility or permission. Must shows necessity. Should and ought to give advice.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Will and shall talk about the future or a promise, and would makes requests polite.

scenes.animation: A rule card: 'Modal + base verb'. Wrong examples crumble with a buzzer: 'She can sings', 'He must to go'. Correct ones glow: 'She can sing', 'He must go'. Note: 'ought to' keeps its 'to'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The big rule: a modal is followed by the base form of the verb. She can sing, not she can sings.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: And no to after most modals. He must go, not he must to go. Ought to is the exception.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So modals are bossy. They don't let the verb change at all!

scenes.animation: Politeness ladder: 'Give me water' at the bottom, then 'Can you give me water?', 'Could you give me water?', 'Would you please give me some water?' at the top. A smiley meter rises with each step.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Modals also control politeness. Could you and would you are more polite than can you.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In Wisdom Paves the Way, the friends speak respectfully to the king. Modals help make that respect sound natural.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So would you please is the VIP version of can you. Noted!

scenes.animation: A practice card: 'You ___ wear a helmet while riding a bike. It is the law.' Options: 'might', 'must', 'could'. 'must' glows green. An 'Exam Tip' sticker: 'Read the clue words: law, rule, advice, perhaps'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Try this. You blank wear a helmet while riding. It is the law.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Law means necessity. So, must!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Right. Exam tip: look for clue words. Law or rule suggests must. Advice suggests should. Perhaps suggests may or might.

scenes.animation: Recap board with three toolbox icons: '1. Modals show ability, permission, necessity, advice', '2. Modal + base verb, no -s, no to', '3. Could and would sound polite'. Zippy politely receives two samosas.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: modals show ability, permission, possibility, necessity and advice.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: always use modal plus base verb, with no s and no to.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: could and would make requests polite.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Could I please have two samosas? See, it worked!

scenes.animation: A marching band where one drummer walks out of step, bumping into everyone. The drummer's shirt says 'VERB', and the band leader's flag says 'SUBJECT'. Zippy blows a whistle.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: That drummer is totally out of step! Who is he?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A verb that doesn't agree with its subject. Today, we fix subject-verb agreement.

scenes.animation: Two scales: 'Singular subject → singular verb: The soldier fights' and 'Plural subject → plural verb: The soldiers fight'. The '-s' jumps from noun to verb and back like a see-saw.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The basic rule: a singular subject takes a singular verb, and a plural subject takes a plural verb.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The soldier fights. The soldiers fight. Notice the s moves. It is on the verb for singular, and on the noun for plural.

scenes.animation: A long sentence appears: 'The box of sweets ___ on the table.' The words 'of sweets' fade to grey, leaving 'The box ... is'. A magnifier highlights the real subject.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Trap one: words between the subject and verb. The box of sweets is on the table.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The subject is box, not sweets. So we use is.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So I ignore the sweets? That's painful, but okay.

scenes.animation: Three more rule cards flip: 'Each / Every / Everyone → singular: Everyone is here.', 'Collective noun as one group → singular: The battalion was ready.', 'Neither... nor → verb agrees with the nearer subject: Neither the boys nor the teacher is late.'

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Trap two: each, every and everyone take singular verbs. Everyone is here.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Trap three: a collective noun seen as one group is usually singular. The battalion was ready, just like Major Sharma's company in Unit 2.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Trap four: with either or and neither nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Neither the boys nor the teacher is late.

scenes.animation: A practice card: 'One of my friends ___ a drummer. (is / are)'. The words 'of my friends' fade; 'One ... is' glows green. An 'Exam Tip' sticker: 'Find the head noun first'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Try this. One of my friends blank a drummer. Is or are?

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Friends is plural, so are! Oh wait... the subject is one. So, is!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Well caught. Exam tip: in editing questions, find the head noun first, then check the verb.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the band now marching in step: '1. Singular with singular, plural with plural', '2. Ignore words between subject and verb', '3. Each, every, collective nouns, neither-nor rules'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: singular subjects take singular verbs, plural subjects take plural verbs.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: ignore the words in between and find the real subject.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: remember the special rules for each, every, collective nouns and neither nor.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: The band is in step. The band are happy? No, is! I'm learning!

scenes.animation: Zippy peers into a crystal ball that shows a train timetable, a rain cloud and a birthday cake. He looks confused as five different future phrases swirl around it.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Neo, why does English have so many ways to talk about tomorrow?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because each way carries a different meaning. Let's sort them out.

scenes.animation: Card 1: 'will + verb: decisions now, predictions, promises'. Zippy hears a phone ring and says 'I'll get it!' Card 2: 'going to + verb: plans and clear signs'. Dark clouds appear: 'It's going to rain.'

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Use will for quick decisions, promises and predictions. The phone is ringing, I will get it.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Use going to for plans already made, or when you can see something coming. Look at those clouds. It is going to rain.

scenes.animation: Card 3: 'present continuous: fixed arrangements' with a diary showing 'Meeting Riya at 5 pm'. Card 4: 'simple present: timetables' with a train board showing 'Train leaves at 6:10'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Use the present continuous for fixed arrangements. I am meeting Riya at five.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Use the simple present for timetables and schedules. The train leaves at six ten.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Present tense for the future? English is sneaky!

scenes.animation: A timeline with a flag marked 'Tomorrow, 8 am'. Card 5: 'future continuous: in progress then', a cartoon of 'I will be travelling'. Card 6: 'future perfect: finished before then', a tick mark: 'I will have finished my homework by 8.'

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Use the future continuous for an action in progress at a future time. This time tomorrow, I will be travelling.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Use the future perfect for an action completed before a future time. By eight, I will have finished my homework.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In Feathered Friend, a space crew would use these all day. By tonight, we will have repaired the purifier.

scenes.animation: A practice card: 'Look at that ball! It ___ break the window!' Options: 'will', 'is going to', 'breaks'. 'is going to' glows green. An 'Exam Tip' sticker: 'Evidence now = going to'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Try this. Look at that ball! It blank break the window.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I can see it coming, so, is going to!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Perfect. Exam tip: if there is present evidence, prefer going to. For a sudden decision, use will.

scenes.animation: Recap board with a calendar and a clock: '1. will: decisions, promises; going to: plans, evidence', '2. present continuous: arrangements; simple present: timetables', '3. future continuous and future perfect'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: will for decisions and promises, going to for plans and clear signs.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: present continuous for arrangements, simple present for timetables.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: future continuous for actions in progress, future perfect for actions completed by a certain time.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: By next week, I will have mastered all of these. Probably.

scenes.animation: A newspaper headline flashes: 'Window Broken!' Zippy, holding a cricket ball behind his back, whistles innocently. Neo raises an eyebrow.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: The window was broken. See? No one's name in that sentence!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Clever. You used the passive voice to hide the doer. Let's learn how it works.

scenes.animation: An active sentence builds: 'Zippy (subject/doer) broke (verb) the window (object).' Then the blocks swap: 'The window (subject) was broken (be + past participle) by Zippy.' Arrows show the object moving to the front.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In the active voice, the subject does the action. Zippy broke the window.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In the passive voice, the object moves to the front and becomes the subject. The window was broken by Zippy.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The formula is a form of be plus the past participle.

scenes.animation: A tense ladder: 'Simple present: is / are + V3 → Tea is grown in Assam.' 'Simple past: was / were + V3 → The report was written.' 'Future: will be + V3 → The prize will be given.' Each 'be' form glows.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The tense stays the same. Only the form of be changes.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Present: tea is grown in Assam. Past: the report was written. Future: the prize will be given.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So be does all the time-travelling, and the verb just stays as V3.

scenes.animation: A science lab. A report card reads: 'The solution was heated. The results were recorded.' A label: 'Passive is common in science and reports'. A small photo of Bibha Chowdhuri's lab from Unit 5 appears.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: We use the passive when the action matters more than the doer, or when the doer is unknown.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That's why science reports love it. The samples were collected. The results were recorded. Unit 5's report on a science exhibition uses exactly this.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: And when the doer is obvious, like the police, we can even drop the by-phrase. The thief was caught!

scenes.animation: A practice card: 'Change to passive: The students planted trees.' The answer builds step by step: 'Trees' → 'were planted' → 'by the students.' An 'Exam Tip' sticker: 'Keep the tense; match be with the new subject'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Try this. The students planted trees. Change it to passive.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Trees were planted by the students. Were, because trees is plural!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exactly. Exam tip: keep the same tense, and make be agree with the new subject.

scenes.animation: Recap board: '1. Active: doer first. Passive: object first', '2. Passive = be + past participle, same tense', '3. Use passive when the action matters more'. The window is shown repaired; Zippy holds a sign 'Window was fixed by me.'

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: in active voice the doer comes first. In passive voice the object comes first.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: passive is be plus past participle, in the same tense.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: use it when the action matters more than the doer.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: The window was fixed by me. That one I'm happy to sign!

scenes.animation: A road full of potholes; Zippy bounces from one hole to the next on a bicycle. He angrily scribbles 'Fix the road NOW!!!' on a scrap of paper and throws it at the municipal office. It bounces off the door.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Nobody is reading my angry note! Why?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because officials respond to formal letters. Poorvi asks you to write two kinds, the letter of enquiry and the letter of complaint.

scenes.animation: A letter template builds from top to bottom with labels: 'Sender's address', 'Date', 'Receiver's designation and address', 'Subject', 'Salutation: Sir/Madam', 'Body: 3 paragraphs', 'Complimentary close: Yours faithfully', 'Name'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Every formal letter has a fixed format. The sender's address, the date, then the receiver's designation and address.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Next, a clear subject line, the salutation Sir or Madam, the body, and the closing, Yours faithfully, with your name.

scenes.animation: An enquiry letter appears addressed to a war memorial office. Highlighted phrases: 'I would like to know...', 'Kindly inform me about...', 'visiting hours, entry fee, guided tours'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A letter of enquiry asks for information. For example, after reading about Major Somnath Sharma, you might ask a war memorial about visiting details.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Ask clear questions politely. I would like to know the visiting hours. Kindly inform me whether guided tours are available.

scenes.animation: A complaint letter to the municipal commissioner builds paragraph by paragraph: 'Para 1: the problem and location', 'Para 2: effects and dangers', 'Para 3: request for action'. Polite phrases glow in green; angry words like 'NOW!!!' are crossed out in red.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A letter of complaint reports a problem. Paragraph one states the problem and the place.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Paragraph two explains its effects, like accidents and traffic jams. Paragraph three requests action.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So I can be firm, but not rude. No capital letters shouting!

scenes.animation: An exam card showing a marking scheme: 'Format', 'Content', 'Expression'. A checklist ticks off: 'subject line', 'polite tone', 'Yours faithfully'. An 'Exam Tip' sticker flashes.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: marks are given for format, content and expression. A missing subject line or wrong closing loses easy marks.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Use Yours faithfully for formal letters, and Yours sincerely or Yours lovingly for letters to people you know.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: And keep the subject line short and specific. For example, complaint about potholes on Station Road.

scenes.animation: Recap board styled as an envelope: '1. Fixed format with subject line', '2. Enquiry: ask polite, clear questions', '3. Complaint: problem, effects, request'. Zippy mails a neatly folded letter; a road roller appears in the distance.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: formal letters follow a fixed format, with a clear subject line.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: an enquiry letter asks polite, clear questions.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: a complaint letter states the problem, its effects, and the action needed.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Look, a road roller! Politeness really works!

scenes.animation: A school corridor. Zippy pins a huge, messy poster covered in doodles: 'THING HAPPENING!! COME!!' Students walk past, confused. Neo sighs and holds up a neat boxed notice.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I made a notice for the science fair. Why is nobody coming?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because it doesn't say what, when or where. Let's learn notice writing, and then report writing.

scenes.animation: A notice builds inside a box: 'Name of school', 'NOTICE', 'Date', 'Heading: SCIENCE EXHIBITION', 'Body: what, when, where, who, contact', 'Name and designation'. A '50 words' badge appears in the corner.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A notice is short and formal. It goes inside a box.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Write the school's name, the word notice, the date and a clear heading. The body answers what, when, where and who can take part.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: End with your name and designation, like Secretary, Science Club. Keep it brief, usually about fifty words.

scenes.animation: The science exhibition happens: stalls, models, a chief guest cutting a ribbon. Then a reporter's notebook opens with the heading 'Report'. Labels appear: 'Heading', 'By-line: by Zippy, Class 8', 'Place and date'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: After the event, you may write a report. A notice announces, but a report describes what already happened.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Start with a heading and a by-line, which is your name. Then add the place and date.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: A by-line! I feel like a real journalist.

scenes.animation: The report body builds in three blocks: 'Intro: what, when, where, who', 'Details: main events, highlights, chief guest', 'Conclusion: result, winners, feedback'. Verbs glow in past tense and passive: 'was inaugurated', 'were displayed'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The body has three parts. An introduction with the key facts, then the main events, then a conclusion with results.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Use the past tense, and often the passive voice. The exhibition was inaugurated by the principal. Over fifty models were displayed.

scenes.animation: An exam card comparing two columns: 'Notice: future event, boxed, short' vs 'Report: past event, by-line, detailed, past tense'. An 'Exam Tip' sticker flashes: 'Don't mix them up!'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: don't mix them up. A notice is about a future event and sits in a box. A report is about a past event and has a by-line.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Also, stay within the word limit. Extra words don't earn extra marks.

scenes.animation: Recap board: '1. Notice: boxed, date, heading, what-when-where', '2. Report: heading, by-line, three-part body', '3. Report uses past tense and passive voice'. Zippy's new neat notice draws a crowd.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: a notice is boxed and short, with the date, heading and key details.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: a report has a heading, a by-line and a three-part body.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: reports use the past tense and often the passive voice.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Notice: Zippy's crowd is huge. Report: Zippy was celebrated by everyone!
